newsitem.title: USA: Ex-New York mobster says he was paid for memoirs.
newsitem.headline: Ex-New York mobster says he was paid for memoirs.

text.p: Mafia turncoat Salvatore "Sammy the Bull" Gravano said on Thursday for the first time he was paid $250,000 for "Underboss," his recently published memoir of life in the mob.

His statement, made during court testimony against accused mob boss Vincent "The Chin" Gigante, followed denials by the book's author Peter Maas and its publisher, HarperCollins, that they had paid the former mobster any money.
Under New York law, Gravano is not allowed to make money from an account of his crimes.

Gravano said his $250,000 advance came from Maas or Maas' company, TJM Productions. He said he also expected royalties from "Underboss," published in April, and was in negotiations to sell the movie rights to it.
For that, he said, "I'd like to get a million dollars."
Gravano, 52, was arrested in 1990 and opted to cooperate with the government rather than face life in prison. He has been in hiding since.
An attorney for Maas, author of such well-known true crime books as "The Valachi Papers" and "Serpico," denied Maas paid Gravano.
"Neither he nor his company has paid Salvatore Gravano any money," attorney Michael Dowd said.
Gravano said he had no contract with HarperCollins. A spokeswoman for the publisher said when the book was published that the company had not paid Gravano anything.

Gravano's statement enraged relatives of his murder victims, whose grisly demises are recounted in detail in his book. Gravano admitted to 19 murders as part of a plea bargain with the government in which he agreed to testify against reputed mobsters.
"I would like a retraction from Peter Maas, who said he never had a deal with Sammy," said Karen Garafolo, whose father Eddie was killed by Gravano in 1990. "I'd like an apology from him."
"Underboss" details life in organised crime, ending with Gravano's arrest and decision to cooperate with prosecutors. His testimony helped convict Gambino godfather John Gotti in 1992.
At Gigante's federal trial in Brooklyn, Gravano identified him as the head of the Genovese crime family. Gigante faces a 21-count murder and racketeering indictment.

"Chin was the boss," Gravano said, appearing nervous at first but visibly relaxing as the day wore on. His hair was slightly grayer and thinner than in his picture on the cover of "Underboss," and he wore a stylish steel-gray suit and small, round glasses.
Gigante sat quietly in a wheelchair, muttering to himself. His attorneys say he has been incapacitated by mental illness for years, but prosecutors say he has feigned illness to avoid prosecution.
Gigante is accused of ordering the killing of seven people and conspiring to kill three others, allegedly to avenge breaches of Mafia protocol such as unauthorised slayings.
